clue.text: Like one who has subscribed to a cause?

definitions.text: Like one who has subscribed to a cause?

parts.words: Like one who has subscribed to a cause?
parts.note: a subscriber who has settled the fee is fully committed as a member of the movement

explanation.surface: Describing a loyal supporter who has signed up to back a campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subscribed' reads as signing up for a cause, but a subscription is also a fee: someone who has handed it over is fully settled and a committed member.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone whose subscription is settled is a fully committed, fee-settled member.

clue.text: A female — uninspiringly dull or passionate?

parts.note: a lame excuse or joke is weak and uninspiring

explanation.surface: A woman is asked whether she is boring or full of fire.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ablaze with feeling is figuratively on fire, burning with emotion.

clue.text: Dispose of fish ball in stew

parts.note: to dump something is to get rid of it
the ling is a long cod-like sea fish

explanation.surface: Instructions to get rid of fish and cook the rest as a stew.
explanation.definitionFit: A suet dumpling is a round lump of dough cooked in a stew or casserole.

clue.text: Sole basis for political campaign

definitions.meaning: a ... sole is the thick raised base of a shoe
a party's set of declared policies on which it campaigns

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sole' looks like the adjective meaning only, but it is the underside of a shoe, and a platform is a very thick one.
explanation.definitionFit: A party manifesto is called its platform, and a thick-soled shoe is a platform shoe.

clue.text: Criminal goes north of the border, with time in prison cut

parts.note: in Scots, the verb 'gang' means go, so he gangs is he goes

indicators.note: cut means the last letter is chopped off the word for a sentence

parts.note: a term is a period served in jail

explanation.surface: A crook heads off to Scotland, having had his prison sentence reduced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'North of the border' means in Scotland, where 'gang' is the word for go; 'cut' removes the last letter of TERM to leave TER.
explanation.definitionFit: A mobster is a violent criminal who belongs to an organised gang.

clue.text: It's pleasant having an extra salutation before departure

parts.note: good weather or a good time is pleasant
in cricket a bye is a run scored without the batter hitting the ball, counted among the extras

explanation.surface: Someone enjoys an extra greeting just before leaving.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a bye is one of the 'extras': runs added to the score that the batter did not hit.
explanation.definitionFit: Farewell is the word said to someone as they leave.

clue.text: Smartening up in dressing-room in guest-house

indicators.note: the first in tells us the answer lies inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Someone tidies themselves in a changing room at a bed and breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across dressinG-ROOM IN Guest-house, using the second 'in' as part of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tidying hair and clothes to look neat is what personal care of appearance involves.

clue.text: Easy-going English bunch, when upset, get bombastic

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the words read from the bottom up

parts.note: a lot is a group or batch of things
to rant is to speak loudly and pompously

explanation.surface: A relaxed English group, once riled, start blustering.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'when upset' means read bottom to top, so the English bunch comes out as TOLE; 'upset' looks like angry, matching the surface of riled people.
explanation.definitionFit: A relaxed, accepting person puts up with things without complaint.

clue.text: Drop leader, replaced as means to rise

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are put back in a different place, a rearrangement

explanation.surface: An instruction to remove a leader and appoint a successor in order to get ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Replaced' signals that the letters of DROP LEADER are reordered.
explanation.definitionFit: A climbing device of cords with rungs lets you go up a ship's side or a tree.

clue.text: Plant fruit tree with sack round

parts.note: a plum is a tree bearing fruit
a bag is a sack
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A fruit tree has a sack wrapped around it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' looks like an instruction to wrap the sack round the tree, but it is simply O, a round letter, added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Plumbago is a flowering shrub, leadwort, often grown for its pale blue blooms.

clue.text: Bit of cream, perhaps, and model will get work

parts.note: a doll is a model of a person
OP, short for opus, is a musical work

explanation.surface: A fashion model is offered a job.
explanation.definitionFit: A blob of thick cream spooned onto a dessert is a typical example of a lump of soft food.

clue.text: Something soothing said to be found in holiday location for top people

parts.note: a balm is a soothing ointment
oral means spoken

explanation.surface: Something calming is said to be found at a posh resort.
explanation.walkthrough: BALMORAL is the Scottish castle where the British royal family take their summer holiday.
explanation.definitionFit: The royal family's Scottish estate is where the monarch spends the summer, so a retreat for the very highest people.

clue.text: Ridiculously inadequate, dire, dreadful — thus the railway?

indicators.note: dreadful suggests the word before it is in a terrible mess, so its letters are jumbled

parts.note: so means thus, in this way
RY is the standard abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: A grumble that the railway service is pitifully poor and awful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dreadful' gives DERI from the word before it; the railway abbreviation is an old British one seen on timetables and maps.
explanation.definitionFit: A derisory offer is so small it invites mockery.

clue.text: Poor chap, floored after count often

definitions.meaning: a boxer knocked down who fails to rise before the referee counts to ten

explanation.walkthrough: In boxing, a fighter who is knocked down and cannot get up before the count of ten has lost.
explanation.definitionFit: A destitute person is a vagrant, and a boxer counted out is beaten and finished.

clue.text: Playing with fire?

parts.note: fire here is gunfire: a mock battle exercise or simulation

explanation.surface: Asking whether someone is taking a dangerous risk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing with fire' is the idiom for taking a foolish risk, but read literally it is a game of shooting.
explanation.definitionFit: A military exercise or strategy simulation stages a battle as a contest.

clue.text: Area adjacent to fighting area roped off

definitions.text: Area adjacent to fighting area roped off

parts.words: Area adjacent to fighting area roped off
parts.note: the seats right beside the roped boxing arena

explanation.surface: Describing a cordoned-off zone next to a battlefield.
explanation.walkthrough: The roped-off fighting area is a boxing ring, and the area next to it is where the best seats are.
explanation.definitionFit: The front seats at a boxing match sit right beside the ropes.

clue.text: Tease the absurd person affecting good taste

indicators.note: absurd says the words are scrambled into a ridiculous order

explanation.surface: Mocking a ridiculous snob who puts on refined airs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Absurd' rearranges TEASE THE.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who claims a refined appreciation of art and beauty, sometimes with affectation.

clue.text: Placed to hear, also able to see

indicators.note: to hear says the word for placed is spoken rather than written

parts.note: sited means located or placed

explanation.surface: Someone is positioned where they can both listen and watch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Placed' gives SITED, which is spoken just like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A person with working eyes, as opposed to a blind one, has vision.

clue.text: Nothing happening in first part of play being performed

parts.note: a play opens with Act I
a show that is on is being staged

explanation.surface: Things stall during the opening scenes of a play's run.
explanation.walkthrough: The first part of a play is ACT I, with I as the Roman numeral one.
explanation.definitionFit: A lack of activity or movement means nobody does anything.

clue.text: Speech problem bringing expression of dismay by Heather

parts.note: heck is a mild exclamation of annoyance
ling is a common name for heather

explanation.surface: A woman named Heather stammers and cries out in alarm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heather' looks like a woman's name, but it is the moorland plant, also called ling.
explanation.definitionFit: Barracking from the crowd is a problem for anyone giving a speech.

clue.text: Some number gathering outside German city

indicators.note: outside says the word for gathering goes around the abbreviation

parts.note: a muster is an assembly of troops
N is a standard abbreviation for an unspecified number

explanation.surface: A crowd assembles outside a city in Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: MUNSTER (Münster) is a city in north-west Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: Münster is a city in Westphalia, Germany.

clue.text: Prepare to sail in top-class vessel — mostly routine task

parts.note: U is the old abbreviation for upper-class
a pan is a cooking vessel

indicators.note: mostly means take all but the last letter of the word

parts.note: a chore is a dull routine job

explanation.surface: Someone on a luxury ship gets ready to depart, mostly as a routine job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' suggests a ship but is a pan; U for upper class is an old British usage; 'mostly' trims CHORE to CHOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Raising the heavy weight that holds a ship in place is how a boat gets under way.

clue.text: Critical description of religion that accounts for congregations dropping off?

definitions.text: Critical description of religion that accounts for congregations dropping off?

parts.words: Critical description of religion that accounts for congregations dropping off?
parts.note: Marx called religion the drug of the masses, and a drug would send churchgoers to sleep

explanation.surface: A sceptic explains why church attendance is falling.
explanation.walkthrough: Karl Marx called religion 'the opium of the people'; 'dropping off' means nodding off to sleep, not declining in number.
explanation.definitionFit: A narcotic made from the poppy, the drug Marx likened religion to.

clue.text: People without say to make contrary statement

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the word for people goes around the short word for say

parts.note: a nation is a people
EG, for example, is what say means when giving an instance

explanation.surface: Citizens who have no voice are forced to contradict.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like lacking, which suits a voiceless people, but here it carries its old sense of outside.
explanation.definitionFit: A denial asserts the opposite of something.

clue.text: Boy in evergreen tree by river

parts.note: the olive is an evergreen

explanation.surface: A lad is up a tree beside a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A common male given name, as in Dickens's orphan Twist.

clue.text: Disaster in air -didn't this land in the Caribbean?

indicators.note: a disaster leaves things wrecked, so the letters that follow are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: An air crash: didn't this plane come down in the West Indies?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disaster in' rearranges AIR DIDN'T; the apostrophe gives no letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The larger island of the twin-island nation off Venezuela in the Caribbean.

clue.text: Hence shortened for that purpose, in old law

definitions.text: for that purpose, in old law

indicators.note: shortened means the last letter of the word for hence is cut off

parts.note: therefore means hence, for that reason

explanation.surface: A legal phrase explained as a clipped form of hence.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic legal word meaning for that thing or in return for it.

clue.text: Lumpy thing is bomb being carried around by lunatic

indicators.note: the bomb word is held inside the word for madman

parts.note: a nut is a crazy person

indicators.note: around means the word for bomb is turned back to front

parts.note: egg is old slang for an aerial bomb

explanation.surface: A madman is carrying a lumpy object that turns out to be a bomb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' gives GGE, which 'being carried' places within the madman; egg is old RAF slang for a dropped bomb.
explanation.definitionFit: A lump of gold or a small chunk of food is a small rough piece.
